definition: A way of expressing how much of a mixture one component takes up, as a share of the total volume. Nitrogen is about 78% of dry air by volume.
msAccepts: (volume of the gas / total volume) × 100%
share of total volume, e.g. 21 cm³ of oxygen in every 100 cm³ of air
msAvoids: confusing with percentage by mass
expecting the percentages to add to exactly 100.00%

definition: Air with all water vapour excluded. The standard composition figures — about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon, 0.04% carbon dioxide — apply only to dry, unpolluted air.
msAccepts: air from which water vapour has been excluded
the basis for the 78/21/1/0.04 composition figures
msAvoids: quoting the composition figures for ordinary humid air
listing water vapour among the four most abundant gases

definition: A gas-tight syringe that measures and transfers accurate gas volumes. Pairs of gas syringes push air back and forth over heated copper in the oxygen-percentage experiment.
msAccepts: gas-tight syringe used to measure and move known volumes of gas
plungers pushed in sequence so air passes over the heated copper
msAvoids: treating it as a container that cannot leak gases in or out
using one to measure liquid volumes

definition: More than enough of a reactant to use up the other reactant completely. The copper, iron or phosphorus in the oxygen-percentage experiments must be in excess so that all the oxygen reacts.
msAccepts: more than enough to react with all of the other reactant
ensures the oxygen is the reactant that runs out first
msAvoids: confusing the excess reactant with the limiting reactant
saying the excess reactant is fully used up

definition: The corrosion of iron in the presence of both oxygen and water, forming rust. Rusting uses up oxygen, which is why damp iron filings can measure the oxygen content of air.
msAccepts: iron reacting with oxygen and water to form rust
oxygen is consumed as iron rusts in damp air
msAvoids: saying iron rusts in dry air alone
using rusting loosely for the corrosion of any metal

definition: A reaction in which a substance burns in oxygen, releasing energy. Elements burn more brightly and rapidly in pure oxygen than in air, which is only 21% oxygen.
msAccepts: burning; reaction with oxygen releasing energy, e.g. Mg, H₂ or S in O₂
oxygen is a reactant in the equation
msAvoids: describing combustion without oxygen as a reactant
restricting the word to burning fuels like coal

definition: The acid formed when sulfur dioxide dissolves in water, H₂SO₃ — not sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄). Sulfur dioxide is also called sulfur(IV) oxide.
msAccepts: H₂SO₃ formed when SO₂ dissolves in water
the '-ous' acid paired with the '- dioxide' gas
msAvoids: writing H₂SO₄ as the product of SO₂ dissolving in water
confusing sulfur dioxide with sulfuric acid

definition: A compound of one element with oxygen. Metal oxides are ionic and usually basic; non-metal oxides are covalent and usually acidic.
msAccepts: compound containing oxygen bonded to one other element
e.g. MgO, CuO, SO₂, CO₂
msAvoids: calling dissolved oxygen gas an oxide
mixing up oxides with carbonates

definition: A metal oxide that reacts with acids to form salts. Usually insoluble in water; the soluble ones dissolve to give alkaline solutions containing OH⁻ ions.
msAccepts: metal oxide reacting with an acid to give a salt (and water)
MgO or CaO dissolving slightly in water to give an alkaline solution
msAvoids: saying all metal oxides dissolve in water
classifying non-metal oxides as basic

definition: A non-metal oxide that reacts with alkalis and bases to form salts. Often soluble in water, giving acidic solutions containing H⁺ ions — CO₂ and SO₂ both behave this way.
msAccepts: non-metal oxide that reacts with alkalis to form salts
dissolves in water to give an acidic solution, e.g. CO₂
msAvoids: saying all non-metal oxides are insoluble in water
classifying metal oxides as acidic

definition: Breaking a compound into simpler substances using heat alone. Most metal carbonates thermally decompose to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide — copper(II) carbonate is the classic example.
msAccepts: splitting one compound into two or more products using heat
CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂ on heating
msAvoids: calling combustion a decomposition
writing heat as a reactant in the equation

definition: A molecule containing carbon and hydrogen only. Petrol is a mixture of hydrocarbons; burning them produces carbon dioxide and water.
msAccepts: compound of carbon and hydrogen atoms only
e.g. octane C₈H₁₈, a component of petrol
msAvoids: including oxygen among a hydrocarbon's elements
calling CO₂ or H₂O a hydrocarbon

definition: A gas that absorbs infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and re-emits it in all directions, warming the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide and water vapour are greenhouse gases; nitrogen and oxygen are not.
msAccepts: absorbs infrared (IR) radiation and re-emits it in all directions
its vibrations change the molecule's polarity, enabling IR absorption
msAvoids: defining it vaguely as a gas that traps heat with no IR mechanism
listing nitrogen or oxygen as greenhouse gases

definition: The radiation a warm surface emits. UV and visible light from the Sun warm the Earth; the surface then radiates infrared, which greenhouse-gas molecules absorb and re-emit in all directions.
msAccepts: radiation emitted by the warm Earth's surface that CO₂ absorbs
re-emission of IR in all directions warms the atmosphere
msAvoids: saying the Sun's incoming radiation is the IR that CO₂ absorbs
saying 'heat' without naming infrared radiation

definition: A molecule with one end slightly negative and the other slightly positive, because one atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly. Water is polar; a vibrating CO₂ molecule becomes polar for an instant.
msAccepts: one end δ+, the other δ−, due to unequal sharing of electrons
polarity also depends on the shape of the molecule
msAvoids: calling a polar molecule an ion
saying polarity requires a full charge separation

definition: The strength with which an atom attracts the electrons in a covalent bond. Oxygen attracts bonding electrons more strongly than carbon or hydrogen do — the origin of polarity in water and in carbon dioxide's bonds.
msAccepts: an atom's ability to attract the shared electrons in a bond
O is more electronegative than C and H, so bond dipoles arise
msAvoids: confusing electronegativity with ionic charge
using the idea for bonds between identical atoms
